texto:
Amazon today said it plans to invest more than €16 billion ($18 billion) in Germany in 2027, with €4.8 billion of that set aside to expand the AWS Europe (Frankfurt) cloud region. The company made the announcement at the Invest in Germany Summit, the federal government's investor conference in Berlin, where chief global affairs and legal officer David Zapolsky appeared alongside Chancellor Friedrich Merz.
In Short
Amazon told the German government it will spend more than €16 billion in Germany next year on data centers, warehouses, satellite internet and TV shows. Amazon calls Germany one of its most important countries, and this money shapes the cloud computers, delivery network and streaming service that German advertisers and sellers rely on. Only the €4.8 billion for cloud computing has a number attached, so most of the plan cannot yet be checked against what actually gets built.
What Amazon committed
The announcement, published on Amazon's corporate news site under the byline "Amazon Staff," is dated October 20, 2026. It describes the €16 billion as spanning "jobs, technology, and infrastructure," and lists four areas: data centers and AI infrastructure, the Amazon Leo satellite network, logistics projects, and "a major new production slate by Prime Video."
The wording of the headline figure varies within the document. The headline and key takeaways say Amazon "will invest €16 billion," while the opening paragraph says it "plans to invest more than €16 billion." One later passage refers to "the €16 billion euros investment," a duplication of the currency in Amazon's own text.
What is missing is a breakdown. Of the €16 billion, only €4.8 billion is assigned to a specific purpose. The remaining €11.2 billion, about 70 percent of the total by PPC Land's calculation, is not split between logistics, satellites, content or anything else. Amazon gives no figure for its Prime Video slate, its fulfillment center upgrades, or Amazon Leo's German operations.
The commitment also sits on top of a larger historic number. According to Amazon, it has invested "over €100 billion" in Germany since 2010. That framing is not new. When Amazon pledged an additional €10 billion for Germany in June 2024, its cumulative figure since 2010 was "over €77 billion." On Amazon's own numbers, that implies roughly €23 billion was added to the running total in a little over two years. Neither figure has been independently audited, and Amazon does not define what it counts as investment.
Much of the surrounding material was also published before the summit. On October 15, five days earlier, Amazon's German press office announced that the company had passed the €100 billion mark and would create more than 3,000 additional logistics jobs from projects already announced. That release listed the same fulfillment center modernizations, the Zweibrücken and Könnern sites, and the 40,000 permanent jobs, 3,000 of them at AWS. It also gave annual figures: more than €14 billion invested in Germany in 2024, according to a September 2025 Amazon release, and €15 billion in 2025, according to the October 15 release. Against that run rate, €16 billion for 2027 is roughly one more year of spending at the level Amazon already reports, rather than an extra sum on top of it. What was new on October 20 was the 2027 total and the €4.8 billion AWS allocation.
The AWS Frankfurt allocation
The €4.8 billion goes to the AWS Europe (Frankfurt) Region, which Amazon launched in October 2014. According to the announcement, the money is planned "in 2027" to meet "customer demand for advanced cloud and AI services."
There is a small inconsistency in timing. The narrative text places the spending in 2027. Stefan Höchbauer, vice president of AWS global sales for Germany and Europe Central, is quoted saying "€4.8 billion is planned to expand the AWS Europe (Frankfurt) Region through 2027." "Through 2027" could mean a multi-year period ending in 2027 rather than a single calendar year. Amazon does not resolve the difference.
"In a fast-moving world, companies need infrastructure they can rely on - secure, available, and built to help them stay ahead," Höchbauer said. "They need the broadest choice of services to meet their individual needs. That is exactly what AWS offers. We will keep investing so that German innovation keeps thriving."
Amazon says it has invested "double-digit billions of euros" in German cloud infrastructure since 2014, including the AWS European Sovereign Cloud, which it says has been generally available since January 2026. PPC Land reported in April that the sovereign cloud's first region sits in Brandenburg and that Amazon had committed more than €7.8 billion to it through 2040. In June 2024, AWS also said it planned €8.8 billion in Frankfurt region investment through 2026, according to PPC Land's coverage of that year's pledge. Amazon's October 15 release adds that €9.6 billion went into the Frankfurt region from 2014 through 2023. The new €4.8 billion reads as the next tranche of that Frankfurt build-out rather than a new site.
Amazon says it employs 3,000 people at AWS in Germany. It also points to apprenticeships run with Siemens since 2023 at data centers in Hesse and Brandenburg, certified by the German chamber of commerce and industry (IHK), and to a Cloud Business Expert (IHK) certification it describes as Germany's first national cloud qualification. The AWS Tech Alliance, launched in December 2023, has reached more than 20,000 students in Germany, according to the company.
Why a cloud region matters to marketers
The scale of AWS spending in Germany is not an abstraction for advertising. AWS is the hyperscaler on which a large share of ad tech, analytics and commerce software runs, and the concentration risk is real: in October 2025, a fault in one region took down 142 services over roughly 15 hours. More capacity in Frankfurt and Brandenburg also feeds the European data residency argument that AWS has been making to companies wary of US jurisdiction, a debate PPC Land has followed through the European Commission's cloud sovereignty framework and T-Systems' appointment of a chief sovereignty officer.
The German figure is also modest beside Amazon's other European commitments. In March, Amazon raised its Spanish plan to €33.7 billion through 2035, up from €15.7 billion, for data centers in Aragon. And it is small next to group spending: Amazon raised its 2026 capital expenditure guidance to about $220 billion in July, most of it for AWS.
Jobs: the same 40,000
Rocco Bräuniger, Amazon's country manager for Germany, said: "We have already created over 40,000 permanent jobs, built more than 100 sites, and invested more than €100 billion in Germany - and we are far from done."
Those headcount figures have barely moved. In June 2024, Amazon said it expected 40,000 permanent employees in Germany by the end of that year and already had more than 100 locations. Twenty-eight months later the description is "over 40,000" and "more than 100 sites." Amazon gives no number of new jobs that the €16 billion itself will create.
The announcement does name logistics projects that it says "account for more than 3,000 new jobs," but it describes these as "already-announced," and the job figure itself was published by Amazon on October 15. The projects are:
- Modernization completed in 2027: fulfillment centers in Bad Hersfeld, Dortmund and Werne.
- Modernization continuing through 2028: Koblenz, Pforzheim and Rheinberg.
- New sites: a fulfillment center in Zweibrücken opening this year, which Amazon says is "already creating jobs," and one under construction in Könnern.
According to Amazon, full-time logistics employees reach an average annual gross salary of €41,600 after two years, plus benefits including up to €4,500 for professional development. The robotics described for these sites are framed as ergonomic support for staff. The page links to a separate Amazon post on its Proteus robot and a €10 billion European fulfillment investment, but gives no German share of that figure.
Amazon is also opening a second robotics and AI research lab in Berlin, which it says doubles its research presence in the city. The roles listed are applied scientists and robotics hardware, software and systems engineers. No headcount is given.
Amazon Leo and Ariane
Amazon Leo, the low Earth orbit satellite network formerly called Project Kuiper, is included in the €16 billion, but its German component is described only in general terms. Amazon says it has secured 24 launches with Arianespace and cites Oxford Economics projecting that Leo's "second-largest economic impact in Europe will be felt in Germany," home to several ArianeGroup sites and the supplier MT Aerospace. The study is commissioned work for Amazon, its figures are not reproduced in the announcement, and the page does not link to it.
PPC Land covered the rebrand from Project Kuiper to Amazon Leo in November 2025, when the network had more than 150 satellites in orbit against a target of 3,200 or more. In April, Amazon agreed to acquire Globalstar to add direct-to-device coverage, by which time Leo had passed 200 satellites. Satellite broadband in low orbit typically runs at round-trip latency of 20 to 40 milliseconds, far below the hundreds of milliseconds of older geostationary links. Amazon does not say when Leo service will be available to German customers or at what price.
Prime Video: 15 productions, no budget
The content element is described in titles, not euros. Amazon says it has produced more than 65 local titles in Germany with partners including UFA, Constantin Film and Bavaria Film, and that more than 15 productions are coming "through the end of 2027." Three are named: Der erste letzte Tag (The First Last Day), based on a Sebastian Fitzek novel; Drive - The Pretenders, starring Lisa-Marie Koroll and Amin Bahmeed; and the show Holey Moley - Minigolf Extreme, hosted by Johannes B. Kerner and Ralf Schmitz with field reporter SelfieSandra.
According to Amazon, European works account for more than a third of everything shown on the Prime Video homepage in Germany. The measure is homepage exposure, not catalogue share, and Amazon does not say how it is calculated.
For advertisers, German originals are inventory. At its first German upfront in September 2025, Amazon said Prime Video reached more than 17 million monthly ad-supported viewers in Germany on CTV and other screens. German series also travel: Prime Video chose the German show Maxton Hall, its most-watched original, to debut AI-assisted lip-sync dubbing in September. Amazon's advertising revenue reached $19.8 billion in the second quarter of 2026, up 26%, though Amazon does not break out Prime Video's share.
Energy and water claims
Amazon describes itself as Germany's largest corporate purchaser of carbon-free energy, with projects totalling more than 1.3 GW of capacity, including offshore wind in the North and Baltic Seas. The company says these projects, once fully operational, are expected to generate enough electricity for the equivalent of more than 1.8 million German households annually. The page links to an earlier Amazon post on what it called Germany's largest power purchase agreement, but does not say how much of the 1.3 GW is already producing power.
On cooling, Amazon says its German data centers use free air cooling with no water roughly 95 percent of the time, and that all planned German data centers will use harvested rainwater for evaporative cooling on the warmest days. The company says it is 75 percent of the way to its goal of being "water positive" by 2030 across its data center operations, supports two water projects in Frankfurt, and has announced a third with NABU, the Nature and Biodiversity Conservation Union, expected to return more than 750 million liters to groundwater a year. These are company-reported figures without published methodology in the announcement.
The rest of the community section lists programs: InCommunities activity near data centers, including coding workshops with TecHeroes, a Think Big Space in Kelsterbach and an EnergyCloud project turning surplus renewable energy into free heating for families in the Frankfurt region; the KiezLab community space at Amazon's Berlin headquarters, which Amazon says offers 1,400 square meters and has served 125 nonprofits; the Goods for Good program, expected to have more than 200 partners by the end of 2026; and a disaster relief hub in Leipzig that Amazon says can deliver supplies across Europe within 72 hours.
The political setting
The announcement came out of the same event at which Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang shared a stage with Merz the previous evening. The summit is the government's attempt to present Germany as a destination for foreign capital, and Amazon's release reads accordingly, with a ministerial quote included.
"Amazon's investment is a clear vote of confidence in Germany as a location for the future," said Katherina Reiche, federal minister for economic affairs and energy. "High-performance data centers are the foundation of the digital economy. With the data wealth of our industry, we also have the potential to become a global leader in industrial AI."
Zapolsky said: "Germany is a hub of innovation and one of the most attractive investment opportunities in Europe. That is why we have invested more than €100 billion here since 2010, and why we plan to invest an additional €16 billion in 2027. We want German businesses, communities, and creators to have the infrastructure and tools they need to compete and grow."
What remains unclear
Several questions are left open by the document. Is the €16 billion capital expenditure, operating spending, or both? How much of it was already committed under earlier announcements, such as the logistics projects described as "already-announced"? Does the AWS figure cover one year or several? And how many new jobs, if any, are expected beyond the 3,000 tied to projects disclosed earlier? Amazon's announcement answers none of these, which leaves €11.2 billion of the headline described by category but not by amount.
Timeline
- October 2014: AWS opens the Europe (Frankfurt) Region.
- December 2023: AWS Tech Alliance starts in Germany.
- June 19, 2024: Amazon pledges an additional €10 billion in Germany, citing over €77 billion invested since 2010 and 40,000 permanent staff by year-end
- September 18, 2025: Amazon says it invested more than €14 billion in Germany in 2024 and over €90 billion since 2010.
- September 2025: Amazon's first German upfront puts Prime Video's monthly ad-supported reach at more than 17 million
- October 20, 2025: AWS outage in one region disrupts 142 services for about 15 hours
- November 13, 2025: Project Kuiper is renamed Amazon Leo
- January 2026: AWS European Sovereign Cloud becomes generally available in Germany, according to Amazon.
- March 2, 2026: Amazon raises its Spanish investment plan to €33.7 billion through 2035
- April 14, 2026: Amazon agrees to acquire Globalstar for Amazon Leo
- July 30, 2026: Amazon raises 2026 capex guidance to about $220 billion
- September 9, 2026: Prime Video applies AI lip-sync dubbing to Maxton Hall
- October 15, 2026: Amazon says it has passed €100 billion invested in Germany since 2010, with €15 billion in 2025 and more than 3,000 logistics jobs from projects already announced.
- October 20, 2026: Amazon commits more than €16 billion to Germany for 2027, including €4.8 billion for AWS Frankfurt, at the Invest in Germany Summit in Berlin.
- 2027: Modernization of Bad Hersfeld, Dortmund and Werne fulfillment centers due to complete.
- End of 2027: More than 15 Prime Video productions due in Germany.
- 2028: Modernization of Koblenz, Pforzheim and Rheinberg due to complete.
- 2030: Amazon's target to be water positive across its data center operations.

Summary
Who: Amazon, represented by David Zapolsky, chief global affairs and legal officer, with Germany country manager Rocco Bräuniger and AWS sales vice president Stefan Höchbauer; federal economy minister Katherina Reiche and Chancellor Friedrich Merz.
What: A plan to invest more than €16 billion in Germany in 2027, of which €4.8 billion is assigned to the AWS Europe (Frankfurt) Region. The remainder covers logistics, Amazon Leo, Prime Video productions and sustainability projects, without amounts. Amazon says it has invested over €100 billion in Germany since 2010, a milestone it first published on October 15, and €15 billion in 2025 alone.
When: Announced today, October 20, 2026, for spending in 2027.
Where: The Invest in Germany Summit in Berlin, with projects in Frankfurt, Brandenburg, Berlin and logistics sites from Bad Hersfeld to Könnern.
Why: Amazon frames the investment as meeting demand for cloud and AI services and expanding logistics and content in one of its most important markets. For marketers, it bears on cloud capacity under the ad tech stack, Prime Video ad inventory in Germany, and Amazon's delivery network, while leaving most of the €16 billion without a disclosed allocation.
